INVOCATION AGENDA 1. Consider Approval of the Minutes for the Planning & Zoning Meeting Held on February 9, 2026. 2. Review and Discuss the Role and Authority of the Planning & Zoning Commission. 3. Review and Discuss the P&Z Commission By-Laws & Hearing Procedures. 4. Review and Discuss Recent Texas Legislation. STAFF COMMENTS ADJOURN MINUTES OF THE SPECIAL MEETING OF THE PLANNING AND ZONING COMMISSION OF THE CITY OF LUFKIN, TEXAS, HELD ON THE 9th OF February 2026 On the 9th of February 2026, the Planning and Zoning Commission of the City of Lufkin, TX convened a Special Meeting in the Council Chambers of City Hall with the following members thereof, to wit: Joseph Ceasar Kevin Cota Jack Ellis Nathan Gann Keisha Williams Monica Peters-Clark Alaina Helton Rosie Maldonado Chairman Commissioner Commissioner Commissioner Commissioner Commissioner City Planner Planning Asst. INVOCATION - The meeting was opened at 5:00 PM with a prayer by Chairman Ceasar. Before proceeding with our P&Z meeting Chairman Ceasar reminded everyone that under the Texas Open Meetings Act the P&Z Commission may only receive public comment and act on matters that have been properly noticed. Therefore, public comments are limited to items on the posted agenda. AGENDA 1. APPROVAL OF MINUTES – Commissioner Williams motioned to approve the January 26, 2026, Planning and Zoning Commission minutes. Commissioner Ellis seconded. The minutes were approved unanimously. 2. Conduct a Public Hearing to consider a request for a Special Use Permit for a Hotel for Lot 4-B, Block 1 of the Garden District Shopping Village Subdivision, Phase IV, totaling approximately 2.8 acres, Request #26-02. City Planner Ms. Alaina Helton presented the item to the Commission. Chairman Ceasar opened the hearing to the Committee for questions. Commissioner Cota asked if the hotel needed a Special Use Permit because of the zoning, and if there were any deed restrictions that would prevent a hotel from being built at this location. Ms. Helton stated yes that hotels in the Local Business zoning district require a Special Use permit. She also stated that there were no deed restrictions preventing a hotel at this location. Chairman Ceasar asked the Commission if there were any more questions, there were none. Chairman Ceasar opened the item for public comment. Mrs. Fawn Zion spoke and came forward with concerns regarding water usage for the hotel and expressed concerns regarding city-wide water usage and the proposed data center to be located outside the city limits. Ms. Aimee Padilla came forward and stated that they are not objecting to the hotel but had concerns regarding the hotel owners using part of their land to connect to an access easement. Chairman Ceaser asked if there were any more public comment. There were none. Chairman Ceaser closed the public hearing and asked if the Committee has any questions. Commissioner Ellis made a statement that the proposed data center is located outside the city limits and would not be an item reviewed by the Commission. Commissioner Green motioned to approve the Special Use Permit for the proposed hotel. Commissioner Ellis seconded the motion. The motion passed unanimously. Staff Comments Chairman Ceasar asked Ms. Helton for any concluding comments from staff. Ms. Helton stated we would be having a P&Z Commission training workshop at our next meeting that would include updates of recent laws passed during the last Texas legislative session and a refresher of the Commission By-Laws. There being no other business, the meeting was closed at approximately 5:11pm. _________________________ Joseph Ceasar, Chairman ATTEST: ____________________________ Alaina Helton, City Planner BY- LAWS AND GOVERNING RULES OF THE PLANNING AND ZONING COMMISSION Eff: 2/13/95 ARTICLE I. Amended 8/5/80 by CC 8/14/80 by P&Z SECTION B. QUORUMS Four (4) members shall be necessary to constitute a quorum of the Commission for all public hearings. A majority of any committee shall constitute a quorum for that committee. SECTION C. NOTICES Written notices of all public hearings before the Commission on proposed zoning changes shall be sent to owners of real property lying within two hundred (200) feet of the subject property not less than ten (10) days before the date set for hearing, said ownership being determined from the last approved City tax roll. Require information from the other departments of the City Government in relation to its 2 work: 5. Attendance at meetings required; absence from meetings. a) All members of the Planning and Zoning Commission shall be obligated to attend all regular meetings of said Commission or its committees unless excused by official action of the Commission or committee at the meeting at which a member may be absent. b) In the event any member of the Commission or its committees shall be absent from three (3) consecutive regular meetings without having been excused for such absence, such member shall automatically cease to be a qualified member of such Commission or committee and 3 the respective body shall certify such fact immediately following any three (3) consecutive unexcused absences to the City Council to inform the City Council of such vacancy and enable the City Council to fill such vacancy by prompt appointment. 3. Members claiming interest in matters under consideration by body. a) It is further declared to be the policy of the Planning and Zoning Commission that said Commission and its committees shall be free of influence of any personal financial interest in a matter under consideration by the respective body shall be present during the taking of action by the respective body nor vote as a member of the respective body. b) Any member having any personal financial interest in a matter before the respective body shall not be prevented from presenting facts or argument as a member of the public c) In those instances where discussion of the respective body and action by the respective body is taken in the absence of the public, any interested member of the respective body should and must be excused and not permitted to return until the action of the respective body and the particular matter at that meeting shall have been concluded. d) In the event the final action of the respective body shall be postponed, tabled or otherwise temporarily disposed of, the interested member or members shall be permitted to return for consideration of other matters pending before the respective body. e) It is further declared to be the policy of this Commission that in the interest of fairness to applicants, proponents, and opponents appearing before this Commission on specific requests for zone changes, annexations, mobile home permits, or subdivision approval, no discussion of the merits or specifics of a case shall be discussed between interested parties and members of the Commission. During Commission meetings no person other than a member of the Planning and Zoning Commission or its staff shall be heard on any matter or proposition coming before the meeting or public hearing, unless invited to speak by the Commission and then he shall come to the bar to speak so as to be heard distinctly by the Commission, giving his name and address. (no provision in Section A shall abrogate the right of postponement set out in Section B). SECTION B. If the applicant desires to postpone, he may do so as follows: 1. All Committees shall present a written report to the Commission, which report may consist of the approval of a similar report prepared by the staff representative. Where a public hearing was held, a summary of the hearing shall accompany the Committee report. Individual Committee reports shall be a part of the journal of proceedings of the Commission. The amendment shall be introduced at one regular meeting and voted upon at the next regular meeting following, and the notice for such regular meeting shall contain a copy of the proposed amendment. 8

During Commission meetings no person other than a member of the Planning and Zoning Commission or its staff shall be heard on any matter or proposition coming before the meeting or public hearing, unless invited to speak by the Commission and then he shall come to the bar to speak so as to be heard distinctly by the Commission, giving his name and address. The preceding sentence shall not apply to answer given by persons present and responding to specific questions by the Commission or staff. ARTICLE VI. WITHDRAWAL, POSTPONEMENT, ENLARGEMENT OR CHANGE IN THE APPLICATION SECTION A. 1. The applicant may, between the date of the filing of the application and the notification by the city of the proposed zone change to the owners of real property lying within 200 feet of the subject property, change, alter, amend, enlarge, partially withdraw or withdraw in full, the application. If the applicant withdraws at this stage of the proceedings, all filing fees will be returned in full. 2. If the applicant withdraws for application after notification by the City, to the adjoining owners of real property lying within 200 feet of the subject property, change, alter, amend, enlarge, partially withdraw or withdraw in full, the application. If the applicant withdraws at this stage of the proceedings, all filing fees will be returned in full. 3. If the applicant withdraws at any time after 72 hours prior to the date set for hearing, the applicant shall forfeit all application fees and there shall be a prohibition against refiling the application for a period of sixty (60) days after the date of withdrawal. (no provision in Section A shall abrogate the right of postponement set out in Section B). SECTION B. If the applicant desires to postpone, he may do so as follows: 1. The applicant shall be allowed one (1) postponement. 2. The request for postponement is made at the time of the hearing on the application, shall be in writing, and shall be delivered to the office of the City Secretary. 3. If the request for postponement is made at the time of the hearing on the application, it 6 may be dictated into the minutes of the Planning & Zoning Commission. 4. No cause need be shown for the postponement. 5. The postponement shall be effective to postpone the hearing on the application until the next regularly scheduled meeting of the Planning and Zoning Commission. 6. If the postponement is requested after the date of the filing of the application, but before the notification by the City of the owners of real property lying within 200 feet of the subject property, no additional fee need be tendered by the applicant. If the request for postponement is made after the notification by the City of the proposed zone change to the owners of real property lying within 200 feet of the subject property, there shall be tendered to the City an additional fee of $25.00. SECTION C. The Commission retains in its discretion, the rights to postpone or reschedule any application at any time prior to or during the hearing on any such application. ARTICLE VII. VOTING PROCEDURE SECTION A. After a motion has been seconded there may follow discussion on the question. After all discussion has been heard and/or objections have been resolved, the Chairman will ask for the vote. A negative vote by a member of the Commission must be accompanied by a statement of his reason for so voting. On completion of the vote, the Chairman shall announce the results and effect of the motion. SECTION B. A member on the prevailing side may change his vote from "Yea" to "Nay" and move to reconsider the question. If the motion is seconded, the matter shall be placed on the agenda for the next meeting, and a vote shall be taken at that next meeting on whether the matter shall be reconsidered. If the motion to reconsider is adopted by majority vote, the original question shall be before the Commission. SECTION C. When a member concludes that a matter before the Commission involved or could involve a conflict of interest on his part or his voting might not be in the public interest, he shall excuse himself from discussion and voting on that matter. He may also excuse himself without conflict of interest by choosing to abstain from voting in accordance with his best judgement. SECTION D. Members may also abstain if they have been absent from the meeting during the public hearing or the discussion, but members shall not leave the meeting table to discuss pending matters with member of the audience, nor shall members of the audience discuss matters with individual Commission members during the meeting. SECTION E. Each member of the Commission including the Chairman shall be required to vote, not withstanding a conflict of interest or when choosing to abstain according to his best 7 judgement, on each item before the Commission and at which that member is present. A majority vote of a quorum shall be adequate for recommendations to the City Council. In the event of a tie vote, the item will be reported to the City Council as a tie, regardless of the vote of the Chairman. ARTICLE VIII. COMMITTEE PROCEDURE Acting in the name of the Commission, all standing and special committees are hereby empowered to conduct public hearings as required by law or as part of their investigation of any matter referred to them. All Committees shall present a written report to the Commission, which report may consist of the approval of a similar report prepared by the staff representative. Where a public hearing was held, a summary of the hearing shall accompany the Committee report. Individual Committee reports shall be a part of the journal of proceedings of the Commission. The amendment shall be introduced at one regular meeting and voted upon at the next regular meeting following, and the notice for such regular meeting shall contain a copy of the proposed amendment. 8 CITY OF LUFKIN REGULAR PLANNING AND ZONING COMMISSION MEETING Monday, February 23, 2026 - 5:00p.m. The Regular Meeting of the Lufkin Planning & Zoning Commission will be convened at 5:00 p.m. on Monday, February 23, 2026, in Room 202 of Lufkin City Hall, 300 East Shepherd Avenue, Lufkin Texas in accordance with Section 551.002 of the Texas Local Government Code. documents.text: From: Subject: To: Sent: Attached: Alaina Helton <ahelton@cityoflufkin.com> FW: Data Center Frequently Asked Questions Rosie Maldonado <rmaldonado@cityoflufkin.com> October 23, 2026 9:42 PM (UTC+00:00) Data Center FAQ.pdf Alaina Helton, AICP Engineering Services City Planner Phone: 936-633-0411 Email: ahelton@cityoflufkin.com City of Lufkin 300 E Shepherd | Lufkin, TX 75901 From: Alaina Helton Sent: Monday, February 9, 2026 9:42 AM To: Alaina Helton <ahelton@cityoflufkin.com> Cc: Rosie Maldonado <rmaldonado@cityoflufkin.com> Subject: Data Center Frequently Asked Questions BCC: P&Z Commission Good afternoon, The City of Lufkin and Angelina County have been approached by a company interested in constructing a data center at the site of the old paper mill on 103. While there are still many details to be developed, it is important we ensure the information shared with the public is correct and factual in nature. As a representative of the City of Lufkin, you may be contacted by our residents regarding this project. The attached frequently asked questions document should cover most of the questions people are asking. If you have any further questions, or someone asks you questions that are not answered here, please don't hesitate to reach out to our Economic development Director, Larissa Philpot-Brown. Alaina Helton, AICP Engineering Services City Planner Phone: 936-633-0411 Email: ahelton@cityoflufkin.com City of Lufkin 300 E Shepherd | Lufkin, TX 75901 DATA CENTER FREQUENTLY ASKED QUESTIONS 1. What is being proposed for the former Southland/Abitibi Paper Mill site? Construction of a data center is being considered at the former paper mill site located just outside of the city limits of Lufkin. The project is currently in the planning phase and has not been approved for construction. The scope and layout are still being developed. 2. Who is the developer? The developer is AmpZ (Amp Z Champion Data Center Holdings). 3. How many jobs would this project create? Current estimates include 30 permanent, full-time jobs once the facility is operational with 500 construction jobs over the first several years. 4. How will this affect residential electric bills? Oncor has different rate classes based on the type of customer. Residential and commercial rates are different classes than industrial users like a data center. The costs incurred by industrial users stay within the industrial rate class. Additionally, any upgrades to facilities dedicated to one customer are paid for by that customer. State law requires facilities like data centers to be one of the first customers “turned off” when the grid needs to conserve power. This enables ERCOT to divert power to more critical facilities when needed. 5. How much water will the data center use? The developer has indicated the facility is being designed with a closed-loop cooling system to minimize water usage. Estimated treated water consumption is 500 gallons per day, which is roughly equivalent to 3 residential homes. 6. Will this impact Lufkin’s water supply? No. The site’s water use is small and is not expected to affect the community water supply. 7. Will there be other impacts? The project developers will be following all state and federal guidelines for development related to clean water, noise, emissions, etc. Given the site’s long-standing industrial use, a data center is expected to generate less impact than many other industrial uses that could develop on the site. The site is located outside the city limits and is not subject to City zoning or permitting. 8. How will this project affect taxes? Due to its large valuation, the project has the potential to positively impact the county tax base. Being outside of the city limits the City of Lufkin will not receive sales or property tax revenue directly from the development.

documents.text: FORMAL STATUTORY BRIEF AND PUBLIC COMMENT RECORD Public Comment on Proposed Amendment No. 1 to the 2027 State Water Plan TO: Texas Water Development Board (TWDB) PROCEEDING: Public Comment on Proposed Amendment No. 1 to the 2027 State Water Plan SUBMITTED BY: Fawn Elizabeth Zion, East Texas Legacy Coalition / Concerned Citizens of Rural Texas DATE: September 22, 2026 I. EXECUTIVE SUMMARY & STATEMENT OF INTEREST This formal brief is submitted to the Texas Water Development Board in connection with the open public comment period for Proposed Amendment No. 1 to the 2027 State Water Plan. This record establishes an exhaustive technical critique of the structural vulnerabilities, reporting deficiencies, and inter-agency blind spots governing industrial water allocation and regional planning across East Texas. Recent executive directives—specifically Governor Abbott’s August 3 instructions to audit data center interconnections, the September 14 directive ordering the TWDB to report on survey compliance enforcement by October 14, and the September 21 directive instructing the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality (TCEQ) to halt data center permit approvals pending an October 19 compliance report—highlight the acute nature of the current crisis. As the Governor’s September 14 directive notes, major industrial water users appear to have committed civil and criminal violations by failing to file mandatory surveys. However, administrative pauses with missing end-dates and narrow reporting windows are insufficient to safeguard Texas water security. Elections pass, temporary pauses expire, and industrial applicants resume unmonitored expansion. What is required is a permanent, airtight statutory and planning alignment ensuring that high-density commercial data centers, crypto-mining operations, and heavy industrial computing complexes are held to strict, enforceable water accounting standards within the State Water Plan before regional aquifers are irreversibly compromised. II. SCOPE OF COMMENT AND REQUESTED AMENDMENT This comment addresses the adequacy of industrial water-demand accounting, water-supply assumptions, and groundwater planning considerations relevant to Proposed Amendment No. 1 to the 2027 State Water Plan. The East Texas Legacy Coalition requests that the TWDB identify whether the amendment adequately accounts for the projected water demands of large industrial computing facilities and other high-volume industrial users in affected East Texas planning areas. Where the amendment relies on incomplete, outdated, or insufficiently disaggregated demand information, the Coalition requests that the Board identify the affected planning assumptions and determine whether supplemental information, revised projections, or additional planning analysis is warranted. East Texas Legacy Coalition — Public Comment, Proposed Amendment No. 1 to the 2027 State Water Plan Page 1 III. AMENDMENT-SPECIFIC FINDINGS Proposed Amendment No. 1 itself documents the gap this comment addresses: • The amendment states that interest in data center water use arose late in the planning cycle and that the TWDB is enhancing data collection for future planning cycles (p. D-2). • Smaller data centers served by municipal providers are counted within municipal demand (p. D-84), and digital infrastructure use is captured either as commercial use in public water systems or as self-supplied manufacturing (p. D-95). • Limited data were available, and none of the 16 regional water planning groups requested digital-infrastructure adjustments to demand projections this cycle (p. D-96). This includes Region I, where Project Lufkin (Amp Z, proposed at 2.1 GW) and HyperDataGrid are under development in Angelina County. • Manufacturing demand is projected using a statewide growth proxy based on historical counts of manufacturing establishments (p. D-95), a method not designed to capture individual facilities of multi-gigawatt scale. • Table C-2 shows Angelina County manufacturing with projected needs equal to 38 percent of total demand in 2030, rising to 45 percent by 2080 (p. D-338). Even before any data center demand is added, the county’s existing manufacturing sector depends on new water management strategies to meet more than a third of its projected demand. • The amendment states that the TWDB has no regulatory authority over permits, groundwater management, drought contingency enforcement, or utility supply contracts (p. D-2). The legislative recommendations in Section VIII of this comment follow directly from that limitation. Accordingly, the Coalition requests that the adopted amendment (1) identify large proposed digital infrastructure projects in Region I as a specific planning uncertainty; (2) state a timeline for the direct facility-level reporting the amendment describes; and (3) direct Region I to evaluate these demands in the 2031 regional water planning cycle. IV. THE REPORTING COMPLIANCE ENFORCEMENT GAP (TEXAS WATER CODE § 16.012(m)) 1. The Statutory Vulnerability Under Texas Water Code § 16.012(m), large-scale commercial and industrial water users are subject to mandatory water use surveys. An entity that fails to timely return the survey is ineligible for board financial assistance and ineligible for TCEQ permits, amendments, or renewals under Chapter 11, and faces Class C misdemeanor liability. However, the Governor’s September 14 directive indicates that major water users appear to have failed to file required surveys. Furthermore, our analysis shows that existing statutory deterrents fail because they do not reach industrial water users who do not rely on TWDB board funding and who acquire groundwater or municipal utility supplies rather than direct Chapter 11 surface water rights. Consequently, while the Class C misdemeanor applies, noncompliance carries no consequence that East Texas Legacy Coalition — Public Comment, Proposed Amendment No. 1 to the 2027 State Water Plan Page 2 prevents a facility from obtaining water or power. When major industrial consumers fail to submit granular, accurate data on water acquisition, consumption, and discharge, the TWDB’s regional water planning models (State Water Plan) and Groundwater Management Area Modeled Available Groundwater (MAG) figures operate blind, masking true aquifer depletion rates. V. REGIONAL WATER PLANNING AND THE MUNICIPAL PASS-THROUGH GAP 1. The Statutory Vulnerability Regional water planning is governed under Texas Water Code § 16.053. Concurrently, local groundwater management is delegated to Groundwater Conservation Districts under Chapter 36. A primary structural flaw in current reporting is the municipal pass-through gap. Massive data centers can bypass direct individual surveys by tapping into municipal water pass-throughs rather than holding direct permits. The City of Lufkin's public FAQ, for example, states Project Lufkin's water use as 500 gallons/day—a figure an opinion column in the Lufkin Daily News sharply questioned against industry benchmarks for multi-gigawatt loads. Where the only public figure comes from the supplying municipality and the end user files no independent survey, such figures go unverified, concealing concentrated stress on shared regional sources like the Carrizo-Wilcox Aquifer (Region I / East Texas Regional Water Plan). Furthermore, coalition calculations estimate that Project Lufkin's full-build water demand would equal approximately 1.76 times the estimated total annual recharge in a defined local recharge area (methodology available on request), underscoring the severe hazard of unrecorded industrial burdens. VI. MEASURING, MONITORING, AND CUMULATIVE IMPACT ANALYSIS 1. The Statutory Vulnerability Annual aggregate totals fail to capture peak-load stress. Facilities report broad yearly averages while omitting peak demand spikes driven by evaporative cooling and secondary indirect water consumption (the massive electrical power generation load required to sustain multi-gigawatt hyperscale footprints). Furthermore, projects are reviewed piecemeal by local bodies, ignoring cumulative regional basin impacts, cooling tower blowdown mineralization, and shell-entity placeholder opacity. VII. REQUESTED FINDINGS AND CORRECTIVE ACTIONS FOR PROPOSED AMENDMENT NO. 1 The East Texas Legacy Coalition respectfully requests that the Texas Water Development Board address the following items in its response-to-comments summary, act on those within the Board's existing authority in adopting Proposed Amendment No. 1, and identify which require action by other agencies or the Legislature: 1 Identify reporting coverage. Publish or provide a summary of the categories of industrial water users subject to water-use surveys under Texas Water Code § 16.012(m), the applicable reporting periods, and the procedures used to identify and address noncompliance. East Texas Legacy Coalition — Public Comment, Proposed Amendment No. 1 to the 2027 State Water Plan Page 3 2 Evaluate municipal pass-through reporting. Determine whether current water-use reporting adequately identifies large industrial end-users obtaining water through municipal and wholesale suppliers, and identify any material data gaps. 3 Improve demand accounting. Evaluate the feasibility of separately reporting withdrawals, purchases, consumption, evaporation, wastewater returns, peak-day demand, and projected full-build demand for major industrial facilities. 4 Assess cumulative regional impacts. Evaluate the combined projected water demands of existing, committed, and proposed large industrial developments drawing from shared water sources, including groundwater and municipal supply systems serving East Texas communities. 5 Improve groundwater planning integration. Identify how new industrial demand is reflected in regional water plans, groundwater availability models, modeled available groundwater values, and desired future conditions. 6 Evaluate drought resilience. Examine whether regional water plans and applicable municipal drought contingency arrangements adequately address competing industrial and public water demands under severe drought conditions. 7 Improve transparency and auditability. Identify what facility-level water-use information can be disclosed under applicable law, explain any necessary confidentiality limitations, and establish transparent procedures for reporting compliance and enforcement outcomes. 8 Evaluate interagency coordination. Identify the information-sharing mechanisms needed among the TWDB, TCEQ, PUCT, ERCOT, groundwater conservation districts, and public water suppliers to ensure that water demand projections are consistent with electricity and industrial development forecasts. 9 Identify legislative recommendations. Specify any statutory changes the Board considers necessary to improve industrial water-use reporting, cumulative impact assessment, water availability review, and enforcement. 10 Document the Board’s response. Address these issues in the planning process and identify which recommendations can be implemented administratively and which require legislative action. VIII. RECOMMENDATIONS FOR LEGISLATIVE ACTION In addition to the administrative actions requested above, the Legislature must enact permanent statutory reforms, including: • Extension of Ineligibility & Mandatory Interconnection Gating: Amending the Water Code to extend § 16.012(m) non-compliance penalties so that failing to file mandatory water surveys results in immediate disqualification from Public Utility Commission (PUC) / ERCOT electrical interconnection queues, state-level tax incentives (such as Chapter 151 sales tax exemptions and Chapter 312 abatements), and groundwater district permits. Enacting statutory requirements modeled on Local Government Code § 232.0032 to ensure no major industrial electrical interconnection or transmission service agreement is finalized without an independent, certified 50-year water supply determination. East Texas Legacy Coalition — Public Comment, Proposed Amendment No. 1 to the 2027 State Water Plan Page 4 • Drought Curtailment Parity: Directing TCEQ by statute to bar municipal drought plans and industrial water supply contracts from exempting large-volume commercial data centers from mandatory community curtailment during regional water shortages. • Tiered Facility-Size Penalties & Transparency: Reforming penalty structures into mandatory, tiered administrative sanctions scaled directly to facility capacity, paired with mandatory beneficial-ownership disclosures and facility-level public transparency. IX. EVIDENTIARY RECORD & SUPPORTING DOCUMENTATION Page citations in Section III refer to Proposed Amendment No. 1 to the 2027 State Water Plan as published by the TWDB for public comment. The factual background, local baseline comparisons, recharge calculations (including the coalition’s 1.76× local recharge calculation methodology), and technical white papers (including the HARC January 2026 white paper and Region I regional water plan data) referenced herein are compiled in the coalition’s master technical file and are available upon request for formal agency review. Respectfully submitted, Fawn Elizabeth Zion East Texas Legacy Coalition East Texas Legacy Coalition — Public Comment, Proposed Amendment No. 1 to the 2027 State Water Plan Page 5

documents.text: Powered Land: How East Texas Water Is Being Committed Out of Public View Oct. 15, 2026 | East Texas Legacy Coalition | @Fawn Elizabeth Zion Executive Overview Angelina County residents keep hearing the same number: about 500 gallons of water a day, roughly three houses. They heard it about the Amp Z data center at the old paper mill. A second data center developer told the groundwater district the same thing. The records tell a different story. That second developer asked for 13 million gallons a year. A power plant planned north of Lufkin asked for 1.5 billion. The city that owns the mill's wells says it won't cap the water it sells, told us in February it had "no responsive documents available for release" about Amp Z's utility needs, and is now asking the Texas Attorney General whether it can withhold records about the project. This piece pulls together records we obtained through public information requests to the county, the city and the Pineywoods Groundwater Conservation District, the reporting of the Lufkin Daily News and The 936, and officials' own words on camera. Documented facts say where they come from. Paragraphs marked Our read are our conclusions from those facts. We are not claiming anyone was bribed, and we are not speculating about any criminal case. We are laying out how decisions about our water and land have been made, and asking the questions the record leaves open. The Numbers Project What the public heard Amp Z data center, About 500 gallons a former Southland mill, day after an initial fill Hwy 103 East What the records show Source A city official privately City FAQ; ETLC told ETLC the site founder's account of a could supply about 20 Feb. 17, 2026 million gallons; city conversation; Amp Z leaders say they won't abatement application; cap use; Amp Z's Lufkin Daily News abatement application lists water needs as "TBD"; water for the on-site gas turbines is unaccounted for. HyperDataGrid data "About 500 gallons per Requested 13 million Pineywoods GCD center, Ben Dunn day" (developer to the gallons a year, about emails Road off Hwy 103 West groundwater district) 70 times that, just under the 15-milliongallon public-hearing trigger. WattBridge power No public figure we Requested 1.5 billion Pineywoods GCD plant, north of Lufkin found gallons a year in March general manager 2026 (about 4.1 million gallons a day); now on hold. The Site The former Southland, later Abitibi, paper mill closed in the late 2000s and has sat idle since. It sits just outside Lufkin city limits, so the city has no zoning or building permit authority over it, and the county has almost none. The property is owned by Verdant Industries and Verdant Industries Realty. The Lufkin Daily News reported that corporate records identify Eric Estes as president of both companies. On camera, Wright said the developers told him they had already spent money on upgrades to bring initial power to the site. The land was not sitting empty. In a December 15, 2025 email to Commissioner Kenneth Jeffrey, County Judge Keith Wright answered a question about Amp Z: "They have the crypo [sic] mining going on. They [have] a third party marketing the land for the data center." The email does not make clear whether "they" means Amp Z or the landowner. Amp Z Champion Data Center Holdings, a Denver-based company, does not own the land. The Lufkin Daily News reported that it holds an option to buy about 1,041 acres from Verdant. In October 2026, Wright described the company as owning land on both sides of Twin Oaks Road. Whether Amp Z has exercised its option is not clear from public reporting. Building the Package Before any official signed anything, the pieces that make an industrial site valuable to a data center buyer were already being assembled: an air permit, a power connection and an assurance of water. ● The Air Permit: The Texas Commission on Environmental Quality issued Verdant an air permit in January 2025 for a power plant with 12 natural gas turbines. The Lufkin Daily News found that the permit's annual particulate limit was set at 249.9976 tons, about 4.8 pounds below the 250-ton line that would have triggered a federal Prevention of Significant Deterioration review, with deeper air analysis and more public involvement. Later reporting by the paper showed TCEQ staff had asked the company whether it could lower its numbers to avoid that review. ● The Water: After a September 2025 meeting at the city's economic development offices, Ryan Smith of Amp Z asked Lufkin City Manager Kevin Gee how the company could "discretely speak to potential customers about the water situation in Lufkin," the paper reported. Gee, who is also president of the Pineywoods Groundwater Conservation District, sent the company a water-availability letter two days later. ● The Engineering: County emails show the Savannah engineering firm Thomas & Hutton invited Wright to a September 30, 2025 meeting with Amp Z executives and the project's engineers, and was working with him on site access by February 2026. Our read: Each of these pieces raises what the site is worth to whoever ultimately builds on it. Wright's description of "a third party marketing the land" fits that picture. The Endorsements The last piece was political support, and it was requested in writing. On November 7, 2025, Mayor Mark Hicks hosted a meeting at the former Temple-Inland boardroom in Diboll. His invitation listed the Estes Family Office, Amp Z executives, Wright, state Rep. Trent Ashby, state Sen. Robert Nichols, U.S. Rep. Pete Sessions, Angelina College President Michael Simon, Lufkin ISD Superintendent James Hockenberry and Lufkin EDC Director Larissa Philpot-Brown. The agenda included "Discussion of utility/Oncor-related issues" and "Brainstorming where and how we can best utilize assistance." According to Hicks, Wright posted a group photo on Facebook that day: "Working together to bring a major opportunity to Lufkin and Angelina County! Stay tuned." Five days later, Raine Cotton of EPG Champion Development, also an Amp Z governing person, emailed the attendees a form letter. It declared "full support" for turning the mill into "a state-of-the-art data center and on-site power generation facility." Cotton wrote that he would compile every signature "into a single version for submission." The letter is addressed "To Whom It May Concern." Nobody has said where it was submitted. According to the Lufkin Daily News, Councilman Robert Shankle signed it November 17, Hicks signed it on city letterhead the next day despite a city policy against business endorsements, and Hockenberry and Simon confirmed signing. Nichols said he did not recall signing, and House candidate Rocky Thigpen said he took no position. Wright returned his on November 18 with two words: "See attached." Our records request shows his copy was signed "Angelina County Judge" and stamped with the official seal of Angelina County. The template Cotton sent had no seal. When the paper asked in September 2026 whether he had signed, Wright did not say. In a later interview with The 936, he acknowledged it: "Yes, we supported it. I supported it." He said he had been given a two-hour window to respond and could not find the letter. We reviewed the Commissioners Court's minutes for Nov. 12, 17, 21 and 25 and Dec. 9, 2025, and found no vote to endorse the project. The Money While the package was being assembled, people connected to the project were giving to officials whose support it needed. All figures below come from campaign records reported by the Lufkin Daily News. Date Sept. 25, 2025 Oct. 9, 2025 Donor Eric Estes Raine Cotton Recipient Amount Rep. Trent Ashby $10,000 Rep. Trent Ashby $10,000 $5,000 Returned Jan. 30, 2026 Not reported by the paper Jan. 28, 2026 Dec. 5, 2025 Eric Estes Dec. 8, 2025 Eric Estes Judge Keith Wright Rep. Pete $3,500 No refund reported Sessions Dec. 9, 2025 Sept.–Dec. 2025 Eric Estes Eric Estes through June 30, 2026 Jan. 28, 2026 Jan. 30, 2026 Rocky Thigpen $5,000 Kristi Skillern $1,000 (district judge campaign; then Lufkin city attorney; now 217th District Judge) The Estes contribution to Ashby is dated the same day Gee sent Amp Z the city's wateravailability letter. The Estes contribution to Wright came 17 days after he signed the support letter and six days before a December 11 call. The next day, Amp Z's director of site development thanked Wright for "the direction" and said its tax consultants would draft an incentive "that aligns with the framework we discussed." The returns came after Eric Estes was indicted on Jan. 23, 2026, in a 2022 shooting death at the mill property. In his 936 interview, Wright said the money was returned "in March" and that "we felt like at that point, 'Hey this is a conflict." Campaign records show his refund was dated Jan. 28. In the same interview, Wright said he got the money "significantly before I was asked to do anything," and that Harold Estes had given to his first campaign. The contribution he returned, $5,000 from Eric Estes, is dated Dec. 5, 2025, 17 days after Wright signed the support letter. Kristi Skillern, who returned Eric Estes's $1,000 on Jan. 30, was appointed judge of the 217th District Court in July 2026. County court records list her as the presiding judge in the murder case against Eric Estes. Separately, The 936 reported that Forge the Future Project with Meta, a Meta-funded political committee, spent $192,827.64 in independent expenditures supporting Ashby in the 2026 primary. That spending was not a direct contribution. To be clear: none of this proves a vote or a signature was bought, and we are not alleging that. It shows who was in the room, who was giving, and when. Managing the Message The Lufkin Daily News broke the story in February 2026. By then, several officials had been engaged for months and had signed letters of support. What followed was a managed rollout, documented in records obtained by the paper. ● The News Release: On February 5, Philpot-Brown sent city leaders a draft release and noted, "I sent this to Amp Z for review." It repeated the developer's projections for investment, jobs and water use. ● The Talking Points: The next morning, hours before Wright's State of the County address, she emailed Wright and city staff a draft for talking points: "Not my best work, but it's the best ChatGPT and I could do in ten minutes." ● The Water Number: The city's FAQ repeated Amp Z's estimate of about 500 gallons a day after an initial fill, compared to three homes. The paper reported that number came from the developer, was not independently verified, and did not address the water the 12 gas turbines could use. Gee later said it was an estimate, not a limit the city would enforce. ● Asking Austin to Stay Out: On February 9, Philpot-Brown sent Gee, Bray, Hicks and Wright "Chamber Days Talking Points" for meetings with Ashby and Nichols' staff. One line urged lawmakers "to resist efforts to get between data center developments and the cities and counties that serve them." When Councilman Jimmy Ford asked basic questions about the cooling system's water use, noise and emissions, Philpot-Brown replied that she would forward them "to Amp Z to get their answers directly." Meanwhile, the record undercuts the reassurances. Verdant's TCEQ air permit application states "No water balance is possible." Amp Z's county tax abatement application, filed in March 2026, listed water, wastewater, electric and gas needs as "TBD" and checked "No" for environmental issues needing to be addressed. The Water Question The City of Lufkin owns the former mill's wells, which it bought in 2009. It is the one local government with a real lever over this project: whether, and how much, water to sell. What residents have been told about that lever does not line up. ● What a city official told us privately: On February 17, 2026, a City of Lufkin economic development official told ETLC's founder that the site could supply about 20 million gallons, but that the city was capping the project's water, and that if the project tried to use more than it had stated, it would have to apply for new permits. The official also said the city had plans in place so the project could not drain the aquifers. This is our founder's firsthand account of that conversation. Separately, Mayor Hicks told The 936 on camera that the paper mill used about 20 million gallons of water a day when it operated. We are not naming the official, who appeared to be trying to protect residents. ● What city leaders said on the record: City Manager Kevin Gee told the Lufkin Daily News the 500-gallon figure was "an estimate, not a limit the city intended to enforce." Mayor Hicks told The 936: "We didn't limit any type of water usage by a user. We don't do that with anyone." ● What the city said about its records: On February 17, 2026, the same day, ETLC asked the city for any utility agreements, impact studies, and communications with Amp Z about utility capacity. Two days later the City Secretary replied that "after conducting a reasonable search," there were "no responsive documents available for release at this time," and cited the economic development exception. In October 2026, answering a later ETLC request, the city said "certain potentially responsive records" had been sent to the Texas Attorney General for a ruling on whether they can be withheld. The same day, Oct. 9, the city referred records from a second ETLC request to the Attorney General as well. City leaders have also been open about wanting a large water customer. In February, Hicks told the Lufkin Daily News that "for years, people have talked about, 'We've got to find somebody to come in here that can use our water." In the 936 interview, the officials described selling water to industry as "a profit center for the city." Our read: Either a written cap and an aquifer protection plan exist, or residents were given a reassurance with nothing behind it. The city now holds records about this project that it has asked the Attorney General for permission to withhold. We have asked the city for any document setting a water cap or aquifer protection plan, and for a copy of its request to the Attorney General. Beyond Amp Z: The Other Draws on the Same Water Amp Z is not the only project. Records ETLC obtained from the Pineywoods Groundwater Conservation District show how water for this wave of development is being lined up across the county, and how often the public is kept out of it. ● Amp Z has filed nothing with the groundwater district: On September 22, 2026, District General Manager Wil Blough wrote that the district had "not been in contact" with Amp Z or Verdant, had received no well permit applications near the mill in two years, and had "not been involved in any talks with this entity over groundwater use." The wells near the property belong to the City of Lufkin or other industries. The district said none of those well owners has asked to increase its permitted pumping. That means Amp Z's water, whatever the amount, runs through the city's existing wells, with no new groundwater permit and no district hearing. ● HyperDataGrid: "About 500 gallons per day" and a 13-million-gallon request: The developers of the second data center site, on Ben Dunn Road off Highway 103 West, bought a 187-acre tract with five water wells through Paluxy LandCo. In an August 5, 2026 email, Blough wrote to developer Clay Roberts that he had said "you did not think you would be using more than about 500 gallons per day." Three of the wells previously held permits totaling 17 million gallons a year. Blough then explained the thresholds: "If you are wanting to keep all 5 and not have a board meeting/public hearing, the cumulative permit total for all five wells needs to be under 15 million gallons per year and pumps cannot be over 69 gpm." Pumps under 17.3 gallons per minute "would not need permits." By September, the developers had asked by phone and email for a lower total of 13 million gallons a year. No action had been taken. Five hundred gallons a day is about 182,500 gallons a year. Thirteen million is roughly 70 times that, and sits just under the line that would require a public hearing. ● A power plant asking for 1.5 billion gallons a year: Blough also disclosed that WattBridge was approved in late 2024 or early 2025 for 80 million gallons a year for a power plant north of Lufkin, which was never drilled. In March 2026 the company changed the plant from peaking to continuous 24/7 operation and requested 1.5 billion gallons a year, about 4.1 million gallons a day. The project went on hold again in July 2026 at the company's request. Separately, Judge Wright said on camera that a power plant the county gave a tax abatement is "talking about producing 1.2 gigawatts" and supplying data centers directly. Our read: The public keeps hearing "500 gallons a day," project by project. The records show the larger volumes sit elsewhere: in city wells the city says it won't cap, in well fields sized just under the hearing trigger, and in the power plants built to feed this load. Margaret Cook of the Houston Advanced Research Center has warned against cooling choices that end up "moving the water use upstream to your power plant," and has called for a measure that counts the water used by a data center and its power source together. Nobody is adding these together. The Turn The public didn't accept the managed version. Residents rallied at Lufkin City Hall in May 2026 and packed the Commissioners Court in June. In an online Lufkin Daily News reader poll, which was not a scientific survey, 79% opposed the project, according to the paper's opinion contributor Sylvia Weathers. Officials repositioned: ● The money went back: The Estes contributions to Wright, Ashby, Thigpen and Skillern were returned in late January 2026, after the indictment. ● The abatement stalled: Amp Z's consultant, KE Andrews, filed for a ten-year abatement in March 2026: 100% in the first year, stepping down 10 points a year. Wright wrote back asking for job, wage, local-spending and conservative water figures. The county later said the application had been rejected and no new one had been submitted. ● The resolution: On July 14, 2026, the Commissioners Court unanimously passed Resolution 010-26, asking the Legislature for authority over setbacks, noise, lighting and water impact statements. Its own text warns that a single data center "can consume millions of gallons of water per day" and that NDAs leave residents learning of projects "only after permits are issued." ● The words softened: Greg Weatherbee of The 936 reminded Wright that at his February State of the County address he had said data centers are coming and people need to accept it. Wright said he had been misunderstood and was talking about global competition, and that his "position has evolved" and he is "more concerned about the impacts of data centers." We credit that shift. Wright and the court did more than most counties have. But some public statements still don't match the record. In August, the Lufkin Daily News reported that Wright reassured Rotarians data centers' water needs should not be a concern, weeks after signing a resolution warning the opposite. On camera, Hicks said that in November 2025 "no one was talking about data centers," though the form letter he was sent and signed that month calls the project "a state-of-the-art data center" in its first sentence. Where It Stands Amp Z has gone quiet. It has not submitted a new abatement application. In August, Gov. Greg Abbott directed the PUC and ERCOT to hold off approving new data center grid connections pending an audit. In September, he ordered the Texas Commission on Environmental Quality to pause all data center permits until that audit is finished, and said the next legislative session will work to eliminate financial incentives for data centers. A second project, HyperDataGrid, is moving faster on Highway 103 West, and Hicks said on camera it will use wells on its own site. The county's remaining leverage is a road-use agreement. On October 13, 2026, commissioners hired attorney Bruce Green for $1,500 to draft one. Wright told KLTV the company wants to close part of a nearby road, which would limit access from Twin Oaks Mobile Home Park to Highway 103. In June, Wright promised at least two public hearings before any deal with Amp Z is finalized. Our read: The fight does not end if Amp Z walks away. The turbine permit, the substation, the water letter and the political goodwill stay with the land. Whoever buys the package next inherits all of it, and none of the questions below go away. What We Still Don't Know Question Does a written cap on the project's water use exist? Is there a plan to protect the aquifer? Record that would answer it Any city document setting a limit, permit condition or protection plan (requested Oct. 2026). What records is the city asking the Attorney The city's ruling request to the Attorney General General to let it withhold? (requested); the AG's decision. What did the city's water-availability letter to The letter itself, reported by the Lufkin Daily Amp Z promise? News but not yet released to ETLC. Where were the signed support letters Cotton's compiled "single version for submitted? submission"; any ERCOT, Oncor or state program filing it was attached to. Has a large-load interconnection been ERCOT large-load interconnection reports; requested for this site, and by whom? Oncor correspondence. Is the 1.2 GW power plant referenced by Judge County abatement filings; TCEQ air and water Wright the same facility as the 1.5B gallon permit logs; ERCOT queue listings. WattBridge project? Has Amp Z exercised its option on the 1,041 Angelina County deed records; the option acres? agreement's terms and expiration. What "framework" for incentives did Wright give Notes, calendar entries, texts and emails from Amp Z on December 11, 2025? that call. Who runs the crypto mining on the site, and on County easement and parcel records; Verdant whose land? and Exacore filings. How much water would the full campus, Turbine design specs; any revised TCEQ or including the gas turbines, actually use? Pineywoods GCD filings. Will the Twin Oaks Road agreement get the Commissioners Court agendas and minutes. public hearings Wright promised? What We're Asking To every official who signed the letter, and to Judge Wright first among them: 1. Withdraw the letters in writing, to the same people you sent them to. Wright said any commitment would require a Commissioners Court vote. The court's minutes for Nov. 12 through Dec. 9, 2025 show no such vote, yet his letter carries the county seal. 2. Say where the letters went. If they were submitted to ERCOT, Oncor, investors or a state program, the public deserves to know. 3. Release the December 11 "framework" and every record of communication with Amp Z, Verdant and EPG Champion, including texts on personal phones. Under the Texas Public Information Act, those are public records. 4. Correct the record on the campaign contribution dates. 5. Hold the hearings. Before any road-use agreement or incentive is approved, hold the public hearings Wright promised, and require a cleanup bond, water reporting and noise limits in writing. To Rep. Trent Ashby, the Republican nominee to succeed retiring Sen. Robert Nichols, and to Rocky Thigpen, the Republican nominee for Ashby's House seat: Gov. Abbott has called on the Legislature to require data centers to report their electricity and water use, and Angelina County has asked for limited authority to regulate them. Put both in a bill in 2027. documents.text: MEMORANDUM: LEGISLATIVE EXECUTIVE SUMMARY TO: Members of the Texas State Legislature FROM: The East Texas Legacy Coalition Fawn Zion - Lufkin, Texas SUBJECT: The Texas Corporate Power Reset Act — A State-Level Bypass of Citizens United THE CRISIS OF SOVEREIGNTY Massive, multi-billion dollar industrial entities are actively leveraging unlimited, anonymous corporate capital to dictate Texas policy and drain critical state resources, such as the Carrizo-Wilcox Aquifer. Under the federal Citizens United ruling, attempting to restrict corporate political "speech" via the Texas Election Code guarantees a federal injunction. We cannot wait for a constitutional amendment to protect Texas land, water, and citizens from out-of-state corporate overreach. THE LEGAL BYPASS: REDEFINING CORPORATE POWER, NOT SPEECH The Texas Corporate Power Reset Act bypasses federal First Amendment challenges by shifting the battlefield from the Election Code to the Business Organizations Code (TBOC). Since 1819 (Trustees of Dartmouth College v. Woodward), the U.S. Supreme Court has held that corporations are artificial entities created strictly by state law. A corporation possesses only the powers that the State expressly grants it in its charter. Texas has the absolute, unassailable sovereign authority to define the powers of the entities it creates, and to define the rules for foreign entities requesting to do business within our borders. If Texas grants a corporation the power to exist, Texas holds the authority to dictate what powers it does not possess. THE LEGISLATIVE MECHANISM Instead of attempting to unconstitutionally restrict corporate speech, this Act simply updates TBOC Section 2.101 (General Powers) to explicitly declare that the State of Texas does not grant corporations the power to expend corporate treasury funds on political elections or ballot measures. 1. Closes the Super PAC Loophole: Corporations will no longer possess the legal power to funnel dark money into independent expenditures. 2. Captures Foreign Entities: Out-of-state corporations operating in Texas must abide by Texas limits on corporate powers, ensuring local Texas businesses and citizens are not outspent by Delaware or California boardrooms. ENFORCEMENT: THE ULTIMATE DETERRENT Fines are merely the cost of doing business for industrial giants. This Act introduces strict, existential enforcement: any entity found violating its authorized state powers by spending treasury money on Texas elections will face the immediate revocation of its certificate of formation or registration. They will lose their legal right to hold state contracts, receive tax subsidies, or transact business in the State of Texas. A BILL TO BE ENTITLED AN ACT Relating to the general powers of domestic entities and foreign entities registered to transact business in this state; explicitly defining and limiting the authority to make political expenditures. BE IT ENACTED BY THE LEGISLATURE OF THE STATE OF TEXAS: SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE. This Act may be cited as the Texas Corporate Power Reset Act. SECTION 2. LEGISLATIVE FINDINGS AND INTENT. (a) The Legislature finds that corporations and domestic entities are artificial beings, invisible, intangible, and existing only in contemplation of state law. (b) The Legislature finds that as creatures of state law, such entities possess only those properties, rights, and powers which the charter of their creation confers upon them, either expressly or as incidental to their very existence. (c) The intent of this Act is to clarify that the State of Texas does not grant, and has never intended to grant, domestic or foreign entities the power to expend corporate treasury funds to influence elections, ballot measures, or political processes within this state. SECTION 3. AMENDMENT TO GENERAL POWERS. Section 2.101, Business Organizations Code, is amended by adding Subsection (b) to read as follows: (b) Notwithstanding any other provision of this code, the general powers of a domestic entity do not include the power to make an independent expenditure, political contribution, or direct campaign expenditure, as those terms are defined by Section 251.001, Election Code, in connection with any state or local election, recall election, or ballot measure in this state. SECTION 4. APPLICATION TO FOREIGN ENTITIES. Subchapter B, Chapter 9, Business Organizations Code, is amended by adding Section 9.056 to read as follows: Sec. 9.056. LIMITATION ON POLITICAL POWERS OF FOREIGN ENTITIES. A foreign entity registered to transact business in this state shall not exercise any power in this state that a domestic entity is prohibited from exercising under Section 2.101(b). SECTION 5. ENFORCEMENT AND PENALTIES. Subchapter E, Chapter 9, Business Organizations Code, is amended by adding Section 9.205 to read as follows: Sec. 9.205. REVOCATION FOR UNAUTHORIZED POLITICAL EXPENDITURES. (a) If the secretary of state receives a final, non-appealable determination from the Texas Ethics Commission or a court of competent jurisdiction that a domestic or foreign entity has violated Section 2.101(b) or Section 9.056, the secretary of state shall immediately revoke the registration or certificate of formation of that entity. (b) An entity whose registration or certificate of formation is revoked under this section is strictly prohibited from holding state contracts, receiving state tax subsidies, or transacting business in the State of Texas. SECTION 6. EFFECTIVE DATE. This Act takes effect immediately if it receives a vote of two-thirds of all the members elected to each house, as provided by Section 39, Article III, Texas Constitution. If this Act does not receive the vote necessary for immediate effect, this Act takes effect September 1, 2027.
